contrasts.note: Milkshake is the answer for ninety-six per cent of the country. Frappe survives in eastern Massachusetts alone, which is why its boundary is short but not sharp: there is very little of it.

contrasts.note: The best known boundary in American English, and one of the softest. St. Louis is a soda island inside pop country, and the map shows the odds sliding rather than switching.

contrasts.note: An almost even national split, which is what makes it useless for locating anybody and interesting to look at: the country divides in half along a frontier hundreds of miles deep.

stages.name: As published
stages.note: One dot per respondent who said “pop”, plotted at their ZIP centroid. This image is the whole surviving record; the coordinates behind it were never released.

stages.name: Ink, un-blended
stages.note: Each dot was drawn in a known colour over white and antialiased, so an edge pixel is a mixture of the two. Solving that mixture recovers what fraction of the pixel was covered, and rejects basemap grey and other answers' colours.

stages.name: Density, saturation corrected
stages.note: Where respondents are dense the dots merge and coverage saturates, which flattens cities. Treating respondents as Poisson within a small window, expected coverage is 1−e^(−λ), so −ln(1−f) undoes it and gives back relative density.

stages.name: What the model uses
stages.note: Smoothed at a bandwidth chosen by cross-validation, restricted to land, and turned into a probability of this answer given the place. This is the surface the quiz above adds up.
